text:
Closest match: [Preference-Drift-Aware Subsequence Learning (September 2026 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12556) learns differentiable soft context boundaries from preference-drift signals, pools preference-coherent subsequences, retrieves relevant historical contexts for recent interactions, and gates recent versus global representations. This directly supports learning which historical contexts remain relevant after preference changes. It does not establish that arbitrary suffixes preserve the full history’s target distribution, and its architecture is generative recommendation rather than NextItNet.

For adaptive convolution, [CAIN (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.12634) uses temporal convolutions to contextualize historical items and generates personalized convolution filters from user profile features. Its dynamic-filter mechanism extends beyond cropping, although its multi-scope aggregation overlaps depth aggregation; profile features are unavailable in this benchmark. [TimeWeaver (2025)](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-8954/13/10/857) also investigates temporal recommendation with adaptive large-kernel depthwise convolution, addressing rigid receptive fields. Neither source establishes a validated boundary-aware NextItNet replacement.

Research implication, rather than a published result: retain one causal NextItNet and learn boundary probabilities from adjacent hidden-state changes and observed timestamp gaps. Gate each dilated convolution tap using elapsed time and intervening boundary probabilities, allowing context-dependent attenuation of obsolete interests. A jointly trained residual path could preserve recurring interests across boundaries. Train gates through next-item prediction without forcing cropped and complete histories to have identical representations. Maintain causal boundary computation at every position; assess whether learned boundaries outperform simple time decay under the fixed macro validation HR@10 protocol.
